paragraphs: Understanding a familiar word in an unfamiliar combination requires more than recognizing patterns seen during training. This paper introduces gSCAN, a benchmark for testing whether language models can apply learned meanings and rules systematically. Its language refers to situations in a grid world, so interpreting an instruction depends on both the words and the surrounding environment.

That grounding makes it possible to test abilities beyond rearranging sentence structures. An adjective such as small must be understood relative to the objects currently present. An adverb such as cautiously must retain its meaning when combined with a new verb. These tasks examine whether a model can reuse familiar linguistic components under changed circumstances.

The authors evaluate a strong multimodal baseline and an existing compositional method. Both fail dramatically in most cases requiring systematic compositional rules. The finding identifies a substantial weakness in the tested methods and makes gSCAN a way to examine precisely where learned language understanding stops transferring to new combinations.
neurips-2020-a-benchmark-for-systematic-.tldr: gSCAN tests language understanding in a grid world and exposes major failures when tested models must generalize familiar meanings to unfamiliar combinations.

paragraphs: Panel count data records accumulated occurrences of recurring events at separate observation times. Behavioral studies collect such data through repeated self-reports, including mobile surveys about smoking. Missing reports make it harder to estimate how event counts develop over time. This paper addresses that problem by estimating the counting process mean function from incomplete observations.

The proposed functional expectation-maximization algorithm works around several existing panel count inference methods. This makes it a wrapper for established approaches rather than a replacement requiring a wholly different analysis. Its main development assumes that reports are missing completely at random. The method also remains robust when the assumed Poisson process does not correctly describe the events.

The theoretical contribution extends parametric expectation-maximization analysis to a general nonparametric setting and provides finite-sample guarantees. Numerical experiments and smoking cessation data illustrate the algorithm's utility. The paper also discusses extensions involving covariates and departures from completely random missingness, distinguishing these directions from the assumption supporting its initial formulation.
neurips-2020-a-robust-functional-em-algo.tldr: A functional EM algorithm estimates average recurrent-event counts from incomplete reports under completely random missingness, with finite-sample guarantees and robustness to Poisson misspecification.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning requires repeated interactions with an environment, making simulation speed an important part of the training process. This paper introduces CuLE, a version of the Atari Learning Environment implemented using CUDA. It moves game emulation onto GPUs and uses their parallel processing capacity to run thousands of games at once.

CuLE also renders game frames directly on the GPU. This avoids a communication bottleneck that arises when CPU emulators must transfer frames to a GPU for learning. The environment scales naturally across multiple GPUs. On a single GPU, the authors report generation rates of up to 155 million frames per hour, a throughput previously achieved using a CPU cluster.

Fast simulation must be paired with a training process that can use the resulting data effectively. The paper therefore examines batching strategies and demonstrates accelerated convergence for A2C with V-trace. Its contribution connects environment implementation with learning performance: increasing the supply of experience becomes useful when the learner is organized to consume that experience efficiently.
neurips-2020-accelerating-reinforcement-.tldr: CuLE runs and renders thousands of Atari games on GPUs, delivering high simulation throughput and accelerating A2C with V-trace through effective batching.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs store facts as relationships between entities, but answering a complex question may require combining several relationships. Large, incomplete graphs make this difficult. Existing embedding approaches place entities in compact spaces, yet the methods described in this paper's motivation support only some logical operations and cannot naturally represent uncertainty.

BetaE represents both entities and queries using Beta probability distributions, whose values lie within bounded support. Neural operators manipulate these distributions to implement conjunction, disjunction, and negation. Supporting negation expands the kinds of questions the framework can express, while the probabilistic representation also provides a way to model uncertainty within the same embedding system.

The authors demonstrate BetaE on arbitrary first-order logical queries across three large, incomplete knowledge graphs. They report relative performance gains of up to 25.4% over existing leading reasoning methods restricted to conjunctive queries without negation. The result combines broader logical coverage with stronger measured performance in the reported evaluations, rather than treating additional query expressiveness as a separate objective.
neurips-2020-beta-embeddings-for-multi-h.tldr: BetaE uses probabilistic embeddings to support conjunction, disjunction, negation, and uncertainty in knowledge-graph reasoning, with reported relative performance gains of up to 25.4%.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning and Q-learning often rely on neural networks to turn complex observations into useful internal features. Those features change during training, making convergence harder to understand than when learning uses a fixed representation. This paper asks whether the evolving representation can itself converge to an optimal one.

For an overparameterized two-layer neural network, the authors prove that both learning methods globally minimize the mean-squared projected Bellman error at a sublinear rate. They also establish convergence of the associated feature representation to the optimal one within the analyzed setting. This goes beyond an earlier neural tangent kernel analysis in which the representation stays near its initial form.

The analysis uses a mean-field perspective, connecting a finite collection of network parameters to a limiting description in an infinite-dimensional Wasserstein space. That mathematical connection allows representation evolution to enter the convergence argument directly. The results extend to soft Q-learning, with an additional connection to policy gradient, while retaining the specific network setting underlying the theory.
neurips-2020-can-temporal-difference-and.tldr: A mean-field analysis proves convergence of temporal-difference and Q-learning, including their learned representations, for an overparameterized two-layer neural network.

paragraphs: Bandit optimization concerns learning from the loss observed for a chosen action, with limited information about alternatives. Performance is measured through regret, which compares the learner's accumulated loss with that of a reference decision called a comparator. This paper develops methods whose regret guarantees adapt to the comparator's norm, a measure of its size.

The intended benefit is that a small comparator norm yields a small regret bound. Such adaptation had previously been studied in the full-information setting. The authors first transfer techniques from that setting to linear bandits, establishing a starting point where the losses have a simpler mathematical form.

They then extend the approach to convex losses that are Lipschitz or smooth. The extension uses a new gradient estimator based on a single observation point, together with carefully constructed surrogate losses. These ingredients connect limited bandit feedback to comparator-sensitive guarantees. The contribution is theoretical: it shows how the strength of a regret bound can reflect the reference decision's scale even when feedback is restricted.
neurips-2020-comparator-adaptive-convex-.tldr: The paper develops linear and convex bandit algorithms whose regret bounds become small when the comparator's norm is small.

paragraphs: Recognizing a class without training examples is especially difficult when classes differ only in small visual details. This paper argues that generating one overall feature representation for an unseen class can overlook the individual attributes needed to distinguish it. The proposed approach instead constructs unseen-class representations from attribute-based features extracted from available training samples.

Composition serves two purposes. It selects features from samples relevant to the attributes being assembled, and it creates diversity by changing which samples supply those features. Rather than compressing the result into a single global summary, the method keeps a dense representation containing fine-grained attribute information. This preserves the details that motivate the approach.

The training scheme uses a discriminative model to construct features that subsequently train that same model, avoiding the need to learn a separate generator. Experiments on DeepFashion, AWA2, CUB, and SUN report significant improvements over the state of the art. The findings support attribute-level composition as a useful way to supply training representations for classes lacking their own examples.
neurips-2020-compositional-zero-shot-lea.tldr: The method recognizes unseen classes by composing diverse, detailed attribute features from relevant training samples and using them to train its classifier.

paragraphs: Counterfactual prediction asks what outcome would occur under a different treatment than the one observed. This paper studies treatments made up of bundles, such as combinations used in recommendation or online marketing. A bundle can be represented by many binary choices, making it difficult to separate treatment effects from confounding patterns in observational data.

The approach assumes that these high-dimensional bundles have an underlying low-dimensional structure. It learns latent treatment representations and uses them in a variational sample re-weighting method called VSR. The re-weighting is designed to remove confounding bias by decorrelating treatments and confounders, changing how much each observed example contributes to subsequent learning.

A predictive model is then trained on the re-weighted dataset. The authors report extensive experiments showing more accurate counterfactual outcome prediction. The central idea is to make bundle adjustment manageable through a compact treatment representation, rather than treating every component combination independently. The assumed latent structure is therefore an explicit part of the method's formulation and of how it addresses the high-dimensional treatment problem.
neurips-2020-counterfactual-prediction-f.tldr: Assuming low-dimensional structure in treatment bundles, VSR reweights observational samples to decorrelate treatments and confounders and improve counterfactual prediction.

paragraphs: A model's prediction reflects its training data, but identifying which examples contributed to that prediction is a separate problem. This paper introduces TracIn, a method for estimating the influence of a particular training example. Its starting point is to track changes in the loss on a test point whenever that training example is used during learning.

Computing that training-history contribution directly can be costly. TracIn makes the calculation scalable through a first-order gradient approximation, saved checkpoints from standard training, and selection of particular neural-network layers. These choices turn the basic idea of tracing loss changes into an implementation built around gradients, checkpoints, and loss functions.

The method applies to models trained by stochastic gradient descent or its variants, without tying the formulation to a particular architecture, application domain, or task. Its significance is a practical route from an individual prediction back to the training examples that influenced it. The authors anticipate usefulness for studying and improving training data; the abstract presents that broader impact as an expectation.
neurips-2020-estimating-training-data-in.tldr: TracIn estimates training-example influence by approximating changes in a test point's loss along gradient-based training using saved checkpoints.

paragraphs: Predicting the movement of several interacting agents requires understanding how their behavior depends on one another. EvolveGraph addresses this by representing relationships through latent interaction graphs. The framework explicitly recognizes and predicts relational structure among heterogeneous agents, making those interactions part of the trajectory forecasting process.

Future behavior can have several plausible outcomes, so the model produces multiple prediction hypotheses. It also allows the interaction graph to evolve adaptively, including when relationships change abruptly. This matters because different ways for the relationships to develop can lead to different trajectories. The framework therefore models changing interactions alongside uncertainty about future movement.

The paper introduces a two-stage training pipeline that improves training efficiency, speeds convergence, and enhances predictive performance. Evaluation covers synthetic physical simulations and multiple real-world benchmark datasets from different areas. The authors report state-of-the-art prediction accuracy in these experiments. Together, the results support treating relationships as changing quantities to be forecast, rather than using them only as a fixed description of the observed scene.
neurips-2020-evolvegraph-multi-agent-tra.tldr: EvolveGraph forecasts multiple plausible agent trajectories by learning interaction graphs that adapt as relationships change, achieving leading accuracy in its evaluations.

paragraphs: Sparse Bayesian models encourage some parameters to be exactly zero, helping select variables and simplify interpretation. Their posterior distributions are usually difficult to compute directly. Mean field variational inference offers a convenient approximation, often with closed-form updates, but this paper shows that its standard use can produce unreasonable results with sparsity-inducing priors such as spike-and-slab.

The main theoretical result concerns mixtures whose component distributions occupy non-overlapping supports: mixtures of exponential families with this property themselves form an exponential family. In particular, a diffuse exponential-family distribution can be combined with a point mass at zero. This places an explicit sparsity mechanism inside a distributional framework useful for deriving inference updates.

Specific distribution choices also preserve conditional conjugacy, retaining a source of analytical convenience. The paper motivates the results through statistical genetics, with connections to generalized least squares, and sparse probabilistic principal component analysis. These examples illustrate how changing the variational formulation can remedy the identified pathology while keeping useful mathematical structure. The theoretical result applies beyond those two applications.
neurips-2020-flexible-mean-field-variati.tldr: The paper remedies failures of standard mean field inference for sparse models by showing how non-overlapping mixtures retain exponential-family structure.

paragraphs: When several graphs come from different groups, two related questions arise: which graphs belong together, and which elements correspond across them? This paper tackles graph clustering and matching jointly. Both problems are NP-hard, but their natural connection motivates a procedure that develops group assignments and correspondences together.

The method uses graduated assignment, maintaining soft matching and clustering decisions over successive iterations. Two separate annealing parameters control the two-way matching constraint and the confidence of cluster assignments. Separating these controls lets the iterative procedure regulate distinct aspects of the joint problem as its assignments develop.

The same technique supports end-to-end learning without ground-truth supervision. A cross-entropy loss compares two matching pipelines, providing a training signal for the convolutional networks that extract keypoint features. On real-world benchmarks, the approach outperforms learning-free algorithms and performs comparably to supervised methods based on matching two graphs. The results connect joint structural reasoning with a way to learn useful matching features without labeled correspondences.
neurips-2020-graduated-assignment-for-jo.tldr: A graduated assignment method jointly matches and clusters graphs and supplies an unsupervised training signal for graph-matching feature networks.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised node classification uses a graph and a limited set of known labels to predict the remaining labels. Sparse supervision and noisy graph connections can leave several plausible classification functions. This paper argues that learning a single deterministic function is too rigid in such settings and proposes Graph Stochastic Neural Networks, or GSNN.

GSNN combines a learnable graph neural network with a high-dimensional latent variable to represent a distribution over classification functions. Rather than committing to one function, it learns a family of possibilities. Amortized variational inference approximates the otherwise intractable joint posterior over the latent variable and missing node labels.

Training maximizes a lower bound on the likelihood of the observed labels, allowing the resulting models to be optimized end to end. Experiments on three real-world datasets report substantial gains over state-of-the-art baselines in different scenarios. The contribution makes uncertainty about the classification function itself part of graph learning, providing additional flexibility when the available labels and graph structure give imperfect evidence.
neurips-2020-graph-stochastic-neural-net.tldr: GSNN learns a distribution over graph classification functions to handle imperfect supervision and graph structure, reporting substantial gains on three real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Deploying neural networks under tight computational constraints can require both a smaller model and resistance to adversarial inputs. These objectives are often studied separately. This paper finds that pruning heuristics developed for ordinary training perform poorly when combined with robust training, motivating a pruning procedure that directly accounts for the robustness objective.

HYDRA lets the training objective guide which network connections should be removed. It expresses pruning as an empirical risk minimization problem and solves it efficiently using stochastic gradient descent. This makes the choice of retained connections responsive to the behavior the robust training process is trying to achieve.

The authors report compressed networks with state-of-the-art accuracy on both benign and adversarial inputs simultaneously. They evaluate CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet using iterative adversarial training, randomized smoothing, MixTrain, and CROWN-IBP. They also demonstrate highly robust subnetworks inside non-robust networks. These findings support coordinating compression with robust learning and show that the robustness of a whole network need not describe every subnetwork it contains.
neurips-2020-hydra-pruning-adversarially.tldr: HYDRA uses the robust training objective to guide pruning, producing compressed networks with leading benign and robust accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A dynamical environment changes through transformations, and those transformations can reveal its underlying organization. Inspired by the use of symmetries in physics, this paper builds a representation-learning framework around the transformations that generate an environment's evolution. Its mathematical foundation is group representation theory, which provides a language for expressing structured transformations.

The authors learn from observations produced by sequential interactions, without supervision identifying the underlying structure. In experiments with explicitly symmetric environments, the framework learns that structure from the observations. An additional disentanglement regularizer encourages interpretable learned representations, connecting the organization of the latent space to the transformations governing the environment.

The method enables accurate predictions over long horizons in the reported experiments. The authors also demonstrate a correlation between prediction quality and latent-space disentanglement. This links an interpretable representation to useful forecasting behavior, while remaining a correlation rather than proof that disentanglement causes better predictions. The work brings symmetry-based descriptions of dynamics into a learning framework evaluated on environments where that symmetry is explicit.
neurips-2020-learning-disentangled-repre.tldr: A group-theoretic framework learns interpretable representations of symmetric dynamical environments and demonstrates accurate long-horizon predictions correlated with disentanglement.

paragraphs: Learning to act in continuous time requires accounting for how an environment evolves between interactions. This paper develops a model-based reinforcement learning framework for semi-Markov decision processes using neural ordinary differential equations. It presents two approaches to modeling continuous-time dynamics, placing the evolution of the environment at the center of policy learning.

The learned models accurately characterize those dynamics and support high-performing policies using a small amount of data in the reported work. Modeling change over time also creates a second opportunity: optimizing the schedule of interactions. The authors develop a model-based method that reduces how often the agent interacts with the environment while maintaining near-optimal performance.

Experiments across several continuous-time domains demonstrate the efficacy of the methods. The contribution therefore concerns both learning effective behavior and choosing when interaction is needed. The abstract contrasts its scheduling capability with model-free methods. Within the proposed framework, a continuous-time dynamics model provides the basis for pursuing performance and lower interaction rates together.
neurips-2020-model-based-reinforcement-l.tldr: Neural ODE dynamics models support data-efficient reinforcement learning and interaction schedules that reduce interaction rates while maintaining near-optimal performance.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders offer convenient encoding networks and fast, tractable sampling, but the paper describes a performance gap relative to other likelihood-based generative models. NVAE investigates whether careful neural architecture design can improve hierarchical VAEs. Its focus complements work on statistical formulations by examining the networks used to implement image generation.

The model combines depth-wise separable convolutions and batch normalization in a deep hierarchy. It also uses a residual parameterization of Normal distributions and spectral regularization to stabilize training. These architectural and training choices form a coordinated design for building a capable hierarchical image VAE.

The authors report state-of-the-art results among non-autoregressive likelihood-based models on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA 64, and CelebA HQ, plus a strong FFHQ baseline. On CIFAR-10, the reported result improves from 2.98 to 2.91 bits per dimension. NVAE also produces high-quality CelebA HQ images. To the authors' knowledge, it is the first successful VAE applied to natural images at 256 by 256 pixels, highlighting the reach of the architectural approach.
neurips-2020-nvae-a-deep-hierarchical-va.tldr: NVAE advances hierarchical VAE image generation through architecture and training design, achieving leading results among non-autoregressive likelihood-based models on several datasets.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder uses an inference network to approximate the hidden-variable distribution associated with an input. Sharing that network across inputs makes inference efficient, but can reduce approximation accuracy compared with optimizing each input separately. Semi-amortized methods refine individual results with iterative gradient updates, which can be computationally expensive.

This paper instead builds a mixture inference model recursively. Each step adds a component intended to reduce the discrepancy between the approximate and true posterior. A functional-gradient argument yields two selection goals: improve the data likelihood lower bound and make the new component different from the existing mixture. The latter encourages useful representational diversity.

Although related to boosted variational inference, the method retains amortized inference suitable for VAEs rather than optimizing a single inference instance. At test time, the mixture network requires only one feed-forward pass. The authors report substantially faster inference than semi-amortized approaches and higher test-data likelihood than state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks. The approach pairs a richer posterior approximation with inexpensive test-time computation.
neurips-2020-recursive-inference-for-var.tldr: Recursive mixture inference improves VAE posterior approximations while retaining a single test-time forward pass, with higher reported benchmark likelihoods.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from images can require substantial data and still generalize poorly to new environments. This paper introduces Reinforcement Learning with Augmented Data, or RAD, a plug-and-play module designed to enhance most reinforcement learning algorithms. It studies augmentation for both image observations and state-based inputs, broadening the approach beyond visual transformations alone.

The work introduces random translation and random amplitude scaling and examines augmentations including cropping, color jitter, patch cutout, and random convolutions. These transformations vary the data used for learning. The authors show that suitable augmentations can allow simple reinforcement learning algorithms to outperform more complex state-of-the-art methods on common benchmarks.

RAD establishes new state-of-the-art results for data efficiency and final performance on pixel-based DeepMind Control Suite tasks and state-based OpenAI Gym tasks. It also significantly improves test-time generalization on several ProcGen benchmarks. The findings make input augmentation a consequential component of reinforcement learning design: changing the training data can improve both how efficiently an agent learns and how well it transfers in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: RAD adds data augmentation to reinforcement learning, improving data efficiency, final performance, and generalization across the reported control benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how many sequential rounds of queries are needed to maximize a monotone gross substitutes function while selecting at most k elements. Queries within a round can be parallelized, so reducing adaptive rounds reduces dependence between stages of computation. The focus is a structured class of valuation functions under a cardinality constraint.

For any constant positive epsilon, the proposed algorithm achieves a 1-epsilon approximation in O(log n) rounds. This gives an exponential parallel-time improvement over previously studied algorithms. A matching-order lower bound shows that obtaining even a constant-factor approximation requires more than o(log n) rounds when queries are restricted to feasible sets of size at most k.

The paper also examines a stronger model permitting queries on larger, infeasible sets. Even there, a non-adaptive algorithm cannot achieve an approximation better than 1/2 plus epsilon. Both lower bounds extend to OXS functions. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets illustrate near-optimal performance and efficiency, complementing the theoretical distinction between parallelizable queries and unavoidable sequential adaptation.
neurips-2020-the-adaptive-complexity-of-.tldr: The paper gives a near-optimal gross substitutes maximization algorithm using logarithmically many adaptive rounds and proves corresponding limits under specified query models.

paragraphs: Factored Markov decision processes describe transitions through components that are conditionally independent. This structure can help organize a reinforcement learning problem, but the particular pattern of dependencies affects its difficulty. The paper studies episodic learning in this setting, assuming that the factorization is already known to the learner.

The authors propose two model-based algorithms with different statistical and computational tradeoffs. The first obtains minimax-optimal regret guarantees for a rich class of factored structures, meaning its worst-case regret matches the best achievable order within that class. The second has better computational complexity while accepting a slightly weaker regret guarantee.

A key ingredient is a newly designed exploration bonus that guides the algorithms' information gathering. The paper also establishes several lower bounds that depend on the factored structure, explaining how structural intricacy can make learning harder. These bounds help assess the algorithms against the difficulty of the problem itself and show why a single generic description of factorization does not fully capture learning complexity.
neurips-2020-towards-minimax-optimal-rei.tldr: With known transition factorization, two model-based algorithms trade computational efficiency against regret, achieving minimax optimality for a rich class of structures.

paragraphs: Learning a function of a graph should account for its structure rather than depend on arbitrary names assigned to its nodes. This paper develops a framework for universal function approximation on graph isomorphism classes, which group together graphs that are structurally equivalent. The framework therefore targets graph-level functions defined over structural identities.

The approach draws inspiration from persistent homology, dependency parsing in language processing, and multivalued functions. The authors prove a collection of desirable theoretical properties and use the framework to enable additional analysis. They also show that it can distinguish classes of graphs that other graph-learning methods cannot separate, connecting approximation power to structural discrimination.

On four established graph classification datasets, the approach achieves state-of-the-art performance. The underlying algorithm has complexity proportional to the number of edges multiplied by the number of nodes. The paper thus combines an expressiveness framework, concrete graph-separation results, and empirical classification performance, while specifying how its computational cost scales with graph size.
neurips-2020-universal-function-approxim.tldr: A framework for universal approximation on graph isomorphism classes distinguishes graph classes missed by other methods and achieves leading results on four classification datasets.

paragraphs: Multiclass support vector machines can be formulated with different training losses. An empirical comparison favored the Weston-Watkins formulation even though its hinge loss is not calibrated to ordinary 0-1 classification loss. This creates a theoretical question: what discrete prediction objective does the Weston-Watkins loss appropriately represent?

The paper introduces an ordered partition loss and proves that the Weston-Watkins hinge loss is calibrated with respect to it. Calibration supplies a principled relationship between the surrogate used during optimization and the discrete loss used to evaluate decisions. The result identifies such a relationship for a different target than simple correct-versus-incorrect classification.

The authors also argue that ordered partition loss is minimally emblematic among discrete losses with this calibration property, giving it a distinguished role in their account. Finally, they use the theory to justify the observed ability of Weston-Watkins SVMs to perform well under massive label noise. The contribution explains an empirical success by identifying the loss structure behind it, without changing the stated lack of calibration to 0-1 loss.
neurips-2020-weston-watkins-hinge-loss-a.tldr: The paper proves that Weston-Watkins hinge loss is calibrated to a new ordered partition loss and uses this theory to explain observed robustness to heavy label noise.

paragraphs: Training a neural network on randomly labeled images is often used to study memorization, but the images still contain structure. This paper investigates what networks learn from that structure despite the meaningless labels. For convolutional and fully connected networks, the authors analytically show alignment between principal components of the network parameters and those of the data.

They examine the effect by first training networks on randomly labeled images and then fine-tuning them on disjoint datasets with either random or real labels. The alignment produces positive transfer: the pretrained networks learn downstream tasks faster than networks trained from scratch. This benefit persists after accounting for simple explanations such as weight scaling.

Other effects can obscure the benefit, including specialization in later network layers. The authors investigate these competing influences across several architectures, including VGG16 and ResNet18, using CIFAR10 and ImageNet. The findings show that random-label training can leave useful structure in network parameters, even when its downstream benefit is not immediately visible in every part of the network.
neurips-2020-what-do-neural-networks-lea.tldr: Networks trained with random labels can learn data-aligned parameter structure that speeds subsequent learning, although competing effects may hide this transfer.

paragraphs: A deployed classifier may be retrained periodically, and successive versions can disagree about the same input. Such changes are particularly troubling when an earlier prediction was correct. This paper studies consistency across model generations and distinguishes it from correct-consistency, which concerns predictions that remain both stable and correct.

The authors prove that an ensemble's consistency and correct-consistency are at least the corresponding averages for its individual learners. They further show a probabilistic improvement in correct-consistency when combining learners whose accuracy is no lower than the average accuracy of the ensemble's components. These statements provide specific ensemble guarantees rather than asserting that every combination must improve every prediction.

To put the theory into practice, the paper proposes an efficient dynamic snapshot ensemble method. Experiments using three datasets and two state-of-the-art deep classifiers validate the theory and demonstrate the method's value. The contribution brings stability across retraining into the evaluation of classifiers and provides an ensemble-based approach for addressing it alongside correctness.
neurips-2020-wisdom-of-the-ensemble-impr.tldr: The paper formalizes prediction consistency across retraining, proves ensemble guarantees, and demonstrates an efficient dynamic snapshot ensemble method.
